abstract.p: An aerofoil wing comprising upper and lower surfaces meeting at the leading and trailing edges and a camber line representing the curvature of the aerofoil comprising at least two regions of substantially linear increases in curvature and wherein the increases in curvature are of monotonically increasing magnitude. Preferably there are three regions of substantially linear increases in curvature.

Aile à profil aérodynamique qui comprend des surfaces supérieure et inférieure se rencontrant au niveau de bords d'attaque et de fuite, et une ligne de cambrure représentant la courbure de l'aile et comportant au moins deux zones d'augmentation pratiquement linéaire de la courbure, les augmentations de la courbure présentant une progression monotone. De préférence la courbure présente trois zones d'augmentation linéaire.

description.p: AIRFOIL TRAILING EDGE
The invention relates to aerofoil sections and in particular to those designed to endure turbulent i.e. high Reynolds number air flows. It has particular application to large civil aircraft.

It is an ever present desire to design aerofoils having improved drag characteristics which at the same time do not diminish lift characteristics to an undesirable level. The parasitic drag on an aircraft includes both viscous drag, resulting from the viscosity of the air, and pressure drag, resulting from an imbalance of pressure acting on the aircraft surfaces. At subsonic velocity the viscous drag is the predominant contributor to the parasite drag of the aircraft. However, as the aircraft approaches Mach 1.0, local regions of supersonic flow develop on the surface of the aircraft. For local Mach numbers nearly equal to 1.0, the air is able to recompress (return to subsonic conditions) without forming local pressure jump discontinuities or shocks on the surface of the aircraft.
It is an object of the invention to provide an aerofoil with even further improved reduced drag characteristics than prior art aerofoils.

The inventors have determined that applying a pressure distribution on the upper surface of an aerofoil with a mild adverse pressure gradient recovery, followed by a rapid increase in pressure just short of the trailing edge, allows aerofoils to be designed which offer lower drag at high Reynolds numbers. The effect of this is to maximise lift to drag ratio by 'pushing" the boundary-layer as hard as possible i.e. close to separation. The inventors have defined a series of upper surface pressure distributions made up of regions of zero pressure gradient, regions of equilibrium, adverse gradient and jumps in pressure. By applying a simplified boundary-layer calculation to the upper surface pressure distributions the inventors have showed that improvements in lift to drag ratios are possible over prior art aerofoils. The inventors have also determined that there was a value of adverse pressure gradient parameter above which the flow would be sensitive to Reynolds number.
The invention consists of an aerofoil wing comprising upper and lower surfaces meeting at the leading and trailing edges and a camber line representing the curvature of the aerofoil comprising at least two regions of substantially linear increases in curvature and wherein the increases in curvature are of monotonically increasing magnitude.

The invention also comprises an aerofoil wing comprising upper and lower surfaces meeting at the leading and trailing edges and a camber line representing the curvature of the aerofoil wherein the negative slope in the aft 4% is more than two times greater than the negative slope at 90% chord.
The invention will be described with reference to the following figures of which:
Figure 1 shows a figure of the desired pressure distribution resulting from flow over an aerofoil according to the invention.
Figure 2 a and b show a design of an aerofoil according to the invention in comparison with a conventional aerofoil.
Figure 3 shows a comparison of surface slope of a conventional aerofoil and one according to the invention.
Figures 4 a - j show various embodiments of the aerofoils according to the invention in terms of their curvature of camber.
Figure 5 shows a generalised representation of the aerofoils of figure 4 in terms of camber curvature.

Figure 6 compares the half thickness distribution for a conventional aerofoil and one embodying the invention
Figure 7, 8, 9, 10 each show graphs of drag coefficient against lift coefficient for two aerofoils aerofoil according to the invention and in comparison with an conventional aerofoil for Mach numbers 0.74 and 0.77 respectively.
Figure 1 1 compares the drag rise boundary for a conventional aerofoil and two aerofoils according to the invention.

Figure 1 shows the desired pressure distribution over an aerofoil as determined by the inventors in order to reduce drag at high Reynolds numbers. The upper aerofoil surface 1 pressure distribution consists of a "sonic" or flat roof top, AB, followed by a mild adverse pressure recovery, BC, which is terminated by a rapid pressure rise, CD. The shape of the aerofoil in the region of AB is constrained to some extent by the need for good supercritical flow development as indicated by the dashed line. The chordwise position of B can vary from 5% to 90% chord. The location of the start of the pressure rise C is at about 98.5% of chord. The rise in pressure coefficient at the rapid pressure jump, CD, has been varied from 0 up to 0.465; the magnitude is chosen to avoid a rapid rise in viscous drag. However for some particular applications it might be advantageous to allow for a higher value. The lower aerofoil surface 2 features a favourable pressure gradient NB', followed by a mild adverse pressure recovery B'C, and terminated by a rapid acceleration CD. The position of B' is determined by location of the maximum thickness of the aerofoil section. Variations on the lower surface design are also illustrated on the sketch, showing a conventional rear loading and local rear loading. The purpose of the local rear loading is to reduce the aerofoil trailing edge angle in order to minimise the risk of increasing the viscous drag level. The rapid acceleration CD, reduces the value of the boundary layer momentum thickness following the growth in the region of the lower surface pressure recovery.

Before the embodiments of the aerofoils according to the invention are described it is necessary to define some terms. The term "camber line" is the line defining the mid point between the upper and lower surfaces of the aerofoil extending from the leading to the trailing edge i.e. zcamber (camber line) = (zuppcr+ziower)/2 where z is the vertical location of the surface at a particular chord position.

The term slope A is defined as dz/dx; and the term curvature K is defined as dΛ/ds =(d2zcambe/dx2)/((l+(zcambe/dx)2)3 2 where x is the chordwise location made non-dimensional by chord length, A is the slope of the camber line at chordwise position x, and s is the distance along the camber line.

Figure 2 a shows an example of an aerofoil according to the invention in comparison with a conventional aerofoil 4 shown in broken lines on the figure. Figure 2b shows in more detail the aft portion of this aerofoil. The section of trailing edge of the novel aerofoil shows a substantial increase camber aft of 97% of chord. However in order to understand the invention it is more appropriate to describe the invention by looking at the slope of the camber.

Figure 3 compares the slope of camber of a known prior art aerofoil 5 and one according to the invention 6 having a reduced level of slope between 50% and 78% of chord followed by an increase in negative slope over the aft 3% of chord. The increase in negative slope at the trailing edge is of the order approaching three times the value at 97% chord as the prior art aerofoil. The negative camber of the novel section increases from -0.175 to about -0.50 at the trailing edge.
Figures 4 a to show the slope against chord position for ten examples of aerofoils which fall within the scope of the invention.

Figure 5 shows a generalised representation of these figures showing three distinct regions of linear negative increase in curvature in the rear half of the aerofoil chord. Thus each aerofoil according to the invention can be described as having three distinct slopes of monotonically linearly increasing negative changes in curvature. The first section 7 comprises generally a shallow linear increase in negative slope as is shown from chord position a to b, the second section 8 a more steep linear increase in slope from c to d and the third section 9 an further even steeper increase in slope from e to f.
The table below gives further information from the slope characteristics of the aforementioned examples with particular reference to the three sections 7, 8, 9 of linear decrease in slope as described above. The table gives the magnitude of curvature of camberline at the start of the first (a-b), second (c - d), and third (e to f) sections respectively, their changes in slope, as well as the chord positions of the start and finish of these regions. The symbol λ denotes the change in curvature of camberline per unit chord.
Aerofoil Slope 1 Slope 2 Slope 3

The table above shows for each aerofoil section the start and end points in terms of percentage chord of each section as well as the curvature at these points and the change of curvature per unit chord. As can be seen the first section of linear decreasing curvature extends over a large proportion of the camber section from generally 65%> chord to approximately 95% chord. The increase in negative curvature is fairly shall and the curvature decreases over this section by an amount between -0.01 and to -0.043. The second increase in negative curvature slope is generally over from the range 95 to 98 % chord to 98 to 99% chord and is a sharper increase in the region of -2 to -28. The third increase in negative slope takes place generally in the last 1% of chord from 99% chord and is a further decrease ranging from -4 to -46.

Figure 6 compares the half thickness distribution zt/c, for a conventional aerofoils and two aerofoils A and B according to the invention, where "c" is the section/wing chord and "t" is section/wing thickness. Aerofoil A has an upper surface pressure distribution with a conventional lower surface rear loading. Aerofoil B has a mild lower surface adverse pressure recovery with the local rear loading. The figures shows that the aerofoils A and B have a significant increase in wing box volume, particularly between from 50% to about 95 % of chord. The difference in wing box volume at 65% of chord are 20% and 30% larger for aerofoils A and B respectively compared to the conventional aerofoil. For aerofoil B the difference between the conventional aerofoil is even more pronounced at 80% of chord having a value of zt/c of about 0.024 and at 87% of chord this value is 0.017 compared with less than 0.01 for the conventional aerofoil; this is about 70% increase in wing box volume. The increase in rear depth offers better flap designs for low speed performance, lower structural weight and increased fuel volume. Therefore, a novel design based on aerofoil B can be exploited to trade lift for an increase in depth and maintain an acceptable aerodynamic performance.

Figures 7, 8, 9, 10 graphs of drag coefficient against lift coefficient for two novel trailing-edge aerofoils 10, 11 respectively at Mach numbers 0.74 and 0.77 respectively. Both novel aerofoils are upper surface designs with differences in the start of the pressure recovery. The start of the pressure recovery is 70% chord for novel aerofoil 10 and 65% chord for novel aerofoil 11. Generally, the drag levels are similar to those for the conventional aerofoil, with the novel
aerofoil 1 showing a slight drag penalty and novel aerofoil 10 a slight drag reduction at Mach 0.74. The design of novel aerofoil 10 gives a higher lift coefficient and has a lower drag at 0.9 CL for Reynolds numbers of 40 x 106 and 60 x 106 . For Mach 0.77, both novel aerofoils show a benefit in terms of reduced drag relative to the conventional section.

Figure 11 shows the improvement in drag rise boundary over a range of civil transport wings comparing novel aerofoil 10, novel aerofoil 11, and a conventional aerofoil. Novel aerofoil 11 has the same upper surface pressure distribution as novel aerofoil 10, but with a mild lower surface adverse pressure recovery with local rear loading close to the trailing edge. Novel aerofoil 11 has traded lift for an increase in thickness over the rear portion of the section. The results show a small drag penalty for novel aerofoil 11 relative to novel aerofoil 10.

The invention covers an aerofoil comprising upper and lower surfaces meeting at the leading and trailing edges and having a chord line extending from said leading and trail edges and a camber line representing the curvature of the aerofoil, wherein aft of the 50%> camber line has three substantially linear increases in negative camber curvature.
The examples given in the figures clarify this claim. In order to define the three regions of substantially linear increase in curvature it is necessary to make some definition

These linear regions are defined as extending over either 20 % of chord or covering a curvature increase of more than -2. It is therefore intended to exclude small increase in negative camber curvature which extend over a small portion of chord length. Additionally the term linear needs to be defined. The term linear for the first section is defined as wherein the maximum deviation in curvature from a straight line drawn along the section over at least 20% of chord is 1 /chord. The term linear for both the second and third section is defined as wherein the maximum deviation in curvature is +/- 1.5 from a straight line drawn line along the section over at least a decrease of +/- 3.

claim.claim-text: 1. An aerofoil wing comprising upper and lower surfaces meeting at the leading and trailing edges and a camber line representing the curvature of the aerofoil comprising at least two regions of substantially linear increases in curvature and wherein the increases in curvature are of monotonically increasing magnitude.
2. An aerofoil wing as claimed in claim 1 wherein there are three regions of substantially linear increases in curvature.
3. An aerofoil as claimed in claims 1 or 2 having a substantially linear increase in curvature over the region of between 60 to 89% to between 96 to 98%o chord.
4. An aerofoil as claimed in claim 3 wherein said linear increase in curvature is between - 0.2 and -1.4.
5. An aerofoil as claimed in any preceding claim having a substantially linear increase in curvature over the region of between 96.0 to 98.0% to between 98 to 99.5% chord.
6. An aerofoil as claimed in claim 5 wherein the second said linear increase in curvature is between -3 and -30.
7. An aerofoil as claimed in any preceding claim having a substantially linear increase in curvature over the region of between 99 to 99.5% to about 99.9% chord.
8. An aerofoil as claimed in claim 7 wherein the third linear increase in curvature is between -3 and -40.

9. An aerofoil wing comprising upper and lower surfaces meeting at the leading and trailing edges and a camber line representing the curvature of the aerofoil wherein the negative slope in the aft 4% is more than two times greater than the negative slope at 90% chord.
10. An aerofoil as claimed in any preceding claim, wherein the aft 4% of chord the slope is less than -0.2.
11. An aerofoil as claimed in any preceding claim wherein the aft 1.5 % of chord line has a value of z/c which is negative.
12. An aerofoil as claimed in any preceding claim wherein between 57% and 68% of chord, the slope is at least 0.05 in a positive direction.
13. An aerofoil as claimed in any preceding claim wherein the slope of camber at 90%> chord is less than -0.8.
14. An aerofoil as claimed in any preceding claim wherein the section thickness at 64%> chord is at least 0.03.
